questions.question: A team says: "Our tool only supports clinicians, who make the final decision, so it cannot be regulated as a medical device." What is the best response?
options: They are right, because only hardware can be a medical device.
They are right, because clinician oversight always removes regulation.
Not necessarily: many frameworks regulate software by its intended use and risk, so they should confirm with their regulatory lead.
Not necessarily: all AI tools are regulated as the highest-risk class everywhere.
questions.explanation: Regulation of software often depends on intended use and risk, even when a clinician makes the final decision, and local rules must be confirmed. The most tempting wrong option is that clinician oversight removes regulation. Human oversight is important, but it does not by itself decide whether software is a medical device.

questions.question: Which is the strongest intended use statement for a capstone evaluation?
options: "The tool uses advanced AI to improve eye health."
"The tool flags retinal photographs from adults with diabetes in primary care that may show eye disease, for review by an eye specialist, who makes the diagnosis."
"The tool detects eye disease with 95% accuracy."
"The tool replaces the need for eye specialists in rural areas."
questions.explanation: A strong intended use statement names what the tool does, for which patients, in which setting, for which user and which decision it supports. The most tempting wrong option is the accuracy statement. A performance figure is not an intended use, and it says nothing about patients, setting or who decides.

questions.question: A tool finds cases with high sensitivity, but almost all of those cases are already found by current practice. What does this mean for its clinical value?
options: Its clinical value is high, because sensitivity is high.
Its clinical value cannot be judged without an RCT, so it should be adopted meanwhile.
Its clinical value is high if the supplier is well known.
Its clinical value is probably low, because it changes little compared with current practice.
questions.explanation: Clinical value means a better outcome compared with current practice, and a tool that repeats what already happens adds little. The most tempting wrong option is that high sensitivity means high value. Performance describes the tool; value describes what changes for patients.

questions.question: Which entry in a risk table is written correctly?
options: Risk: lower performance for patients who speak regional languages. Mitigation: check performance by language in silent mode before use. Owner: quality lead.
Risk: the tool may be wrong. Mitigation: staff will be careful. Owner: everyone.
Risk: data breach. Mitigation: none needed because the likelihood is low.
Risk: alert fatigue. Mitigation: to be decided later. Owner: to be decided later.
questions.explanation: A good entry names a specific risk for a defined group, a concrete mitigation and a named owner. The most tempting wrong option is the data breach entry. Low likelihood does not remove the need for a mitigation when severity is high.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of silent-mode testing in a safe implementation plan?
options: To train staff to use the tool before launch.
To reduce the cost of the tool.
To replace the need for monitoring after launch.
To check local performance, including by patient group, on real current cases without affecting patient care.
questions.explanation: In silent mode the tool runs on real cases, but clinicians do not see its outputs, so local performance and equity can be checked with no risk to patients. The most tempting wrong option is that it replaces later monitoring. Performance can change after launch, so monitoring must continue.
